label: Daniyel (Daniel) — Part 1 — Chapters 1–6
summary_plain: Daniyel and his companions are taken captive to Babylon. They refuse the king's food and drink — they keep the covenant dietary laws in exile. Daniyel interprets Nevukhadnetzar's dream of a great image — head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron and clay. A stone cut without hands strikes the image and becomes a great mountain filling the whole earth. Chananyah, Misha'el, and Azaryah refuse to bow to the golden image and are thrown into the furnace — YHWH delivers them. Daniyel reads the writing on the wall for Belshatzar. Daniyel is thrown into the lion's den — YHWH shuts the lions' mouths.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from eight DSS Daniel manuscripts (4QDan-a through 4QDan-e, 1QDan-a, 1QDan-b, and 6QDan) and the Orit Ge'ez. The DSS Daniel manuscripts are among the oldest found at Qumran. Chapters 1-6 are court narratives set in Babylon demonstrating that covenant identity and YHWH's sovereignty are maintained even in the deepest exile under the most powerful empire. The dietary refusal (ch 1), the furnace (ch 3), and the lion's den (ch 6) are all tests of covenant faithfulness under imperial pressure.

key_terms.definition: The Hebrew exile in Babylon whose visions and faithfulness under empire are recorded in the book bearing his name; his name means 'YHWH is my judge'; he and his companions Hananyah, Misha'el, and Azaryah refuse to compromise their covenant practice under Babylonian rule.

The Babylonian king who conquers Yerushalayim and exiles the Yehudim; appears in Daniyel 1-4; in ch.4 he is humiliated — driven mad for seven years — until he acknowledges YHWH as the Most High who rules the kingdoms of human beings.

Hebrew names given by the Babylonians to Hananyah, Misha'el, and Azaryah — Daniyel's three companions who refuse to bow to Nebukhadnetsar's golden image and are thrown into the furnace but emerge unharmed; Daniyel 3.

The furnace into which Shadrakh, Meshakh, and Aved-Nego are thrown for refusing to bow to the golden image (Daniyel 3); they emerge unharmed; Nebukhadnetsar sees a fourth figure in the fire 'like a son of the gods' — the text does not identify who this figure is.
The Babylonian name given to Daniyel (1:7); in ch.4 Nebukhadnetsar calls on Daniyel by this name to interpret his dream of the great tree; the name links Daniyel to the Babylonian deity Bel (Marduk).

The mysterious inscription that appears on the palace wall during Belshazzar's feast (Daniyel 5): MENE MENE TEKEL UFARSIN; interpreted by Daniyel as YHWH's verdict: the king's days are numbered, he has been weighed and found wanting, his kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians; Belshazzar is killed that night.

The four Aramaic words written on the wall at Belshazzar's feast (Daniyel 5:25): MENE = numbered/counted (twice for emphasis); TEKEL = weighed; UFARSIN = divided/broken. Daniyel interprets: YHWH has numbered the days of Belshazzar's kingdom; he has been weighed and found wanting; his kingdom is divided and given to Media and Persia.

Daniyel 6: Daniyel continues praying to YHWH three times daily despite a royal decree forbidding it; he is thrown into the den of lions but emerges unharmed; King Darius acknowledges the living Creator who delivers. The story parallels the furnace narrative of ch.3 — YHWH's protection of covenant faithfulness under empire.

The king in Daniyel 6 under whose rule the lions' den incident occurs; not independently identified outside the book of Daniyel; the text presents him as ruling Babylon after Belshazzar's death; he issues the decree against prayer, then deeply regrets it, and honors YHWH after Daniyel's deliverance.

key_terms.term: The Dream of the Great Tree (ch.4)
key_terms.definition: Nebukhadnetsar's dream of a great tree reaching to heaven, cut down on the command of a watcher/holy one until seven seasons pass; Daniyel interprets it as applying to Nebukhadnetsar himself — he will be humiliated, living like a beast for seven years until he acknowledges that YHWH rules the kingdoms of human beings and gives them to whomever he chooses.

faq.question: What is the main theme of Daniyel chapters 1-6?
faq.answer: Covenant faithfulness under empire. Daniyel and his companions live as exiles in Babylon under Nebukhadnetsar, Belshazzar, and Darius, and in each narrative they face a choice: compromise their covenant practice to survive, or remain faithful to YHWH at great personal risk. In each case, YHWH protects the faithful — the food test, the furnace, the lions' den — and the foreign king is ultimately confronted with YHWH's sovereignty.

faq.question: What does the four-metal statue in Daniyel 2 represent?
faq.answer: Nebukhadnetsar dreams of a great statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay. Daniyel interprets it as a succession of empires, each less glorious than the last, ending with a stone cut without hands that strikes the statue and becomes a great mountain filling the earth. The stone represents YHWH's kingdom that will ultimately overturn all human empires.

faq.question: What does the furnace narrative in Daniyel 3 teach about covenant faithfulness?
faq.answer: The three companions refuse to bow to Nebukhadnetsar's golden image, knowing the penalty is death. Their statement — 'our Creator is able to deliver us... but if not, we still will not serve your gods' — is one of the most direct expressions of covenant faithfulness in the Hebrew scriptures: YHWH may or may not intervene physically, but the covenant community does not compromise either way. YHWH does deliver them, and the fourth figure in the fire remains unidentified.

faq.question: What is the significance of Nebukhadnetsar's humiliation in Daniyel 4?
faq.answer: Nebukhadnetsar is at the height of his power, claiming credit for Babylon's greatness, when YHWH strikes him with madness. He lives like a beast for seven years until he acknowledges: 'The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.' His restoration and declaration (4:34-37) is one of the most explicit acknowledgments by a foreign king of YHWH's sovereignty in the entire Hebrew corpus.

faq.question: What does MENE MENE TEKEL UFARSIN mean?
faq.answer: The four Aramaic words on the wall (Daniyel 5:25-28): MENE = numbered/counted (twice, for emphasis) — YHWH has numbered the days of Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end; TEKEL = weighed — Belshazzar has been weighed in the balances and found wanting; UFARSIN = divided/broken — his kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. Belshazzar is killed that same night.

faq.question: What is the connection between Daniyel's visions and the broader DSS tradition?
faq.answer: The DSS Qumran community preserved and intensely studied the book of Daniyel. Fragments from at least eight copies of Daniyel were found at Qumran (4QDaniel manuscripts), making it one of the most heavily represented books in the DSS collection. The community interpreted Daniyel's visions — especially the seventy weeks and the Son of Man — as applying to their own situation under foreign empire, treating Daniyel's visions as a framework for understanding their own period.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Hebrew and Aramaic sections of Daniyel?
faq.answer: Daniyel is unique in the Hebrew scriptures: it switches languages mid-text. Daniyel 1:1-2:4a is in Hebrew; 2:4b-7:28 is in Aramaic; 8:1 returns to Hebrew. This bilingual structure has been interpreted as deliberate: the Aramaic court narratives (chs 2-7) concern universal empires and are written in the lingua franca; the Hebrew visions (chs 8-12) are addressed to the covenant people specifically. The DSS fragments preserve both languages.

faq.question: Who is Darius the Mede in Daniyel 6?
faq.answer: Darius the Mede (6:1) is presented as ruling Babylon after Belshazzar's death. This figure has not been independently confirmed in Babylonian records; historians have proposed various identifications (Cyrus, a Median commander, a composite figure). The book of Daniyel presents him as a real king who issues the prayer decree, is distressed by Daniyel's condemnation, and honors YHWH after the deliverance. The text is primarily theological: regardless of the historical question, the narrative establishes YHWH's authority over the Medo-Persian transition of power.

faq.question: What does the lions' den parallel with the furnace narrative?
faq.answer: Both stories follow the same pattern: (1) a faithful Hebrew refuses a command that compromises covenant loyalty; (2) the foreign king is personally unwilling but bound by the law he has established; (3) the Hebrew is thrown into lethal danger; (4) YHWH protects the faithful; (5) the foreign king acknowledges YHWH's sovereignty in a formal decree. The two narratives bracket the Babylonian and Medo-Persian transitions, demonstrating that YHWH's protection of the covenant community persists across changing empires.

faq.question: What is the significance of Daniyel's refusal to eat the king's food in ch.1?
faq.answer: Daniyel resolves not to defile himself with the king's food (1:8). This is a covenant-identity act: the food regulations of the Hebrew community marked separation from surrounding nations and dedication to YHWH. Eating the king's food would signal assimilation into Babylonian culture. YHWH honors Daniyel's faithfulness: after ten days of vegetables and water, the four youths are healthier than those eating the royal food, and YHWH gives them knowledge, wisdom, and — specifically to Daniyel — the ability to understand visions and dreams.

faq.question: What does the book of Daniyel have to do with the seventy-year exile and return?
faq.answer: Daniyel 9 (in Part 2) is the clearest engagement with the seventy-year period — Daniyel reads Yirmeyahu's prophecy of seventy years (Yirmeyahu 25:11-12) and prays in response, then receives the vision of seventy weeks of years (490 years). The ch.1-6 narratives establish the exile setting: Daniyel lives through the transition from Babylonian to Medo-Persian rule, positioning the covenant community at the threshold of the promised return while remaining faithful throughout.
